**Golden-hour ending**

Casual handheld movement with subtle camera shake and imperfect human operation. Genuine human reactions and spontaneous interactions. The entire 30-second generation should feel like one continuous, coherent day in Bandung captured by a real friend — not a collection of disconnected AI-generated scenes.

🇬🇧 LONDON BOOKSHOP ACCUSED OF GIVING HITLER’S MEIN KAMPF “DANGEROUS NEW POWER”

Aafaq Bookstore on London’s Edgware Road has been found selling Arabic-language copies of Adolf Hitler’s Mein Kampf, reportedly displayed with a photograph of Hitler giving the Nazi salute.

The book’s ideological importance is beyond dispute: Mein Kampf laid out central elements of Hitler’s National Socialist worldview and foreshadowed the genocidal policies and wars that followed. More than 12 million copies were sold before the fall of Nazi Germany.

The issue, argues writer Robin Schäfer, is not simply whether the book is available—but how it is presented and contextualized.

Schäfer writes:

“There is a difference between preserving a poisonous historical text and peddling it.”

He points to Germany’s Institute for Contemporary History (IfZ), which produced a critical edition with more than 3,500 scholarly annotations designed to expose Hitler’s distortions and place his claims against historical research.

Schäfer argues:

“Availability is not the same as endorsement.”

But he warns that an unannotated translation, particularly one marketed with Hitler’s image in a Nazi salute, can strip away the historical context and potentially turn the text into a vehicle for modern propaganda.

“There is no scholarly reason to reproduce Hitler’s image in mid-salute.”

And his conclusion is blunt:

“It is imperative to deconstruct Hitler and his propaganda thoroughly, thereby depriving this dangerous book of its symbolic power. Aafaq Bookstore has done the opposite.”

The debate is not about banning history. It is about whether a text responsible for helping articulate a genocidal ideology should be presented as serious historical material—or marketed with the very imagery that helped create its cultic power.

Mein Kampf in Arabic is precisely what they teach in the Muslim countries, and this is why it’s now the Islamic Republic of Britain.

I’ve been using @sleepagotchi for a while, and what keeps me interested is how much the product has evolved.

It started with the sleep to earn idea, but it feels like they’re building something much broader now.

Instead of opening an app, checking a sleep score, looking at a few charts, and moving on, the AI Sleep Coach actually gives you some context around your night. It points out changes, explains what might have caused them, and gives you a couple of practical things to try.

That part feels far more useful to me than the usual “sleep more” advice.

What I find even more interesting is how the different coaches are starting to connect. Sleep data can lead into conversations around energy, stress, daily habits, food, and recovery. The Meal Planner and Shopping Agent are still being rolled out, but you can already see where the product is heading.

The privacy side is also worth mentioning. Your biometric data stays on your phone, while anything processed externally is anonymized and not retained. That matters when you’re dealing with something as personal as health and recovery data.

Personally, I’ve noticed small changes. I’m more deliberate about when I go to bed, I pay more attention to recovery instead of just counting hours, and the feedback makes it easier to stay consistent.

And yes, 2.2 million users is impressive.

But I think the bigger story is whether people keep opening the app every day because it genuinely helps them. That kind of retention says far more than points, rewards, or a virtual pet ever could.

This Paper is one of the cleverest solutions I’ve seen for fixing Diffusion Alignment.

If you’ve worked with RLHF or Reward Backprop on DiTs, you must be tired of delayed feedback. 

Evaluating only the final image makes credit assignment a total nightmare. 

You either run out of VRAM trying to unroll the full trajectory, or you fight insane gradient variance with online RL.

The authors solve this by sticking learnable, position-free "register tokens" into a frozen DiT. 

Instead of waiting until step 50, these registers pull dense reward signals directly out of noisy intermediate latents. 

It turns out you can accurately judge trajectory quality surprisingly early in the denoising process.

What makes this paper stand out is how practical the applications are:

1-For training: Their distillation setup (RG-OPD) skips standard policy gradients entirely and hits the same alignment performance while using up to 33x fewer GPU hours. That’s huge for making alignment accessible.

2-For inference: You can use their Reward-Guided Sampling (RGS) to steer generation live off these register gradients thus improving both prompt adherence and visual quality without retraining or touching model weights.

It’s a super clean, well thought-out approach that addresses both the compute bottleneck and inference control at once. 

Definitely worth a read if you're working on generative models:
https://t.co/tfkSPmYwiU

A quick reality check for anyone worried that OpenAI is about to watermark every ChatGPT response.

OpenAI has signed the EU transparency code and has been expanding provenance systems, but the confirmed rollout so far is focused mainly on generated images and supported audio through C2PA/SynthID.

OpenAI has researched invisible text watermarking and developed experimental methods for it, but it has not announced plans to deploy text watermarks in ChatGPT. In fact, OpenAI has previously acknowledged that this could unfairly affect people who use AI for legitimate writing assistance, especially non-native speakers.

So for now:

→ Image/audio watermarking: confirmed
→ Text watermarking research: confirmed
→ Invisible watermarks coming to ChatGPT text: speculation, not an announced feature

No reason to panic yet.
